newsitem.title: SOUTH AFRICA: FEATURE-Zulu king celebrates quarter century of troubled reign.
newsitem.headline: FEATURE-Zulu king celebrates quarter century of troubled reign.

text.p: The king of the Zulus celebrates 25 years on the throne this month and preparations are being made for what promises to be a colourful silver jubilee.
But all is not well in the Zulu kingdom.

King Goodwill Zwelithini, 48, is a direct descendant of the celebrated 19th-century warrior king Shaka, founder of the Zulu nation and ruler of one of Africa's biggest ethnic groups of more than nine million people.
Some say he is a spendthrift who has become irrelevant in South Africa's new democratic order.

King Goodwill was enthroned on December 3, 1971, as the eighth Zulu monarch, and under South Africa's former apartheid system he broke with tradition and rallied his people behind his uncle Chief Mangosuthu Buthelezi's drive for Zulu autonomy.

But since white minority rule was swept away and President Nelson Mandela's African National Congress (ANC) took charge of the country after elections in April 1994, the Zulu nation has been disunited and the king's role blurred.
At the heart of the violent divide are almost two years of soured relations between Buthelezi and his nephew.

King Goodwill fell out with Buthelezi soon after the democracy vote, when he set out to become a neutral figurehead. He abandoned party politics, saying he wanted to work for Zulu unity, peace and development.
To ordinary Zulus his move was long overdue. He had been an effective vote-puller for Buthelezi's Inkatha Freedom Party (IFP), which won power in the Zulu heartland of KwaZulu-Natal.
ACCUSED OF SELLOUT TO ANC
But conservative Zulus in Inkatha saw the king selling out to the ANC, which they often accused of being biased in favour of the Xhosa people.
Scores have died in KwaZulu-Natal clashes between ANC and IFP-supporting Zulus, and between rival Zulu camps who sympathised with either Buthelezi or the king.

In April King Goodwill's niece was abducted and hacked to death in a raid at one of the monarch's six palaces by alleged IFP warriors, while one of his five queens and her daughter survived the ordeal with heavy scars.

But despite the grief, the king in October held talks with Buthelezi over their quarrel. The meeting was part of the fragile truce in the Zulu heartland initiated by local IFP and ANC leaders last June.
Analysts say the encounter heralded a normalisation of relations between the king and his 300-odd chiefs -- without whom he can hardly function.

Since the king's move to political neutrality, most KwaZulu-Natal chiefs have sided with Buthelezi and his IFP, sometimes splitting their clans apart in the process. King Goodwill has called on them to rise above party politics too.
Last year the Zulu monarch set up a peace and development trust to ease the suffering of his impoverished people. But now he is under attack for living a life of opulence.
His closest aide, Prince Sifiso Zulu, quit in November as his spokesman and adviser. He said the king had failed to show his worth in South Africa's new democratic order.
The prince said Goodwill, who has about two dozen children, is seen by taxpayers as a "liability" not as an asset in a country still rising from the ashes of divisive rule.
King Goodwill has an annual budget of 17 million rand ($3.7 million) from Mandela's government, which is channelled through the KwaZulu-Natal administration.
PALACES BEING RESTORED
Six million rand is being spent for renovations on the king's six palaces. Five million rand is being budgeted for the jubilee, for which no date has yet been set, officials said.
One royal insider, who is also a Zulu prince, said criticism of the king's expenditure was baseless.
"The money he gets amounts to nothing because he still has to take care of everyone, including many queens and children of his forebears, even the public who come destitute to cry to him," he said.
Analysts say that while many loyal Zulus take pride in King Goodwill, regardless of whether he does anything for his money, he lacks the drive to engage himself more in public life.
Early last year Goodwill rejected an Inkatha plan to install him as South Africa's constitutional monarch, like his British counterparts.

KwaZulu-Natal's provincial constitution says the king is a custodian of traditional and customary law, a mediator in disputes among his chiefs, who often have clans fighting over boundaries and grazing lands.
King Goodwill also has the duty to open and address sessions of the provincial parliament and meet foreign dignitaries, with the hope of winning investments for KwaZulu-Natal.
Mary de Haas, an anthropologist from the University of Natal, says that whether the Zulu monarch is relevant or not in the new order is an idle question. He is not going to disappear.
"If you were to try to demote the king in any way, now or in the future, it would be politically too dangerous because that would be used as a rallying point," she said.
"People would immediately say 'You see? The Zulus are under threat from the Xhosas.'"
